title: Chapter 21: The Sunny Pair 3
content:
Chapter 21

"Oh? So there are man-eating monsters prowling around?" Wei Wuxian asked.

He’d heard variations of this exact local campfire tale at least a thousand times and personally put down over a hundred of the supposed beasts; the premise was honestly boring.

The vendor, leaning hard into the dramatic flair, dropped his voice to an ominous cadence. "You'd better believe it! Word has it that tucked away in those ridges sits a 'Man-Eating Castle,' home to flesh-devouring horrors. Anyone who stumbles inside gets picked completely clean—not a splinter of bone left behind! Not a trace of a corpse, without exception! Terrifying, right?"

That explained why Jin Ling was lingering around town. After missing his shot at the Soul-Consuming Goddess back on Dafan Mountain, he was undoubtedly gunning for whatever monster was supposedly haunting Xinglu Ridge to prove himself.

Wei Wuxian gasped with dramatic, deadpan horror. "Terrifying indeed! But tell me: if they leave not a splinter of bone behind, and not a single corpse has ever been recovered, how on earth does anyone know they were eaten in the first place?"

The vendor sputtered for a beat before coughing. "Someone... well, someone saw it, obviously!"

"Color me impressed," Wei Wuxian marveled. "Didn't you just swear that anyone who stumbles inside gets devoured clean down to the marrow, with zero exceptions? So who on earth spread the rumor? What kind of legendary hero witnesses that whole feast and walks away with their skin intact just to gossip about it?"

The vendor’s face twitched. "That’s just how the story goes! How am I supposed to know?!"

"Then do you know how many people have actually gone missing on Xinglu Ridge?" Wei Wuxian pressed, leaning in. "When were they eaten? What were their ages? Men? Women? Names? Addresses?"

"No clue."

"And you're the Know-It-All of Qinghe? Truly?"

The peddler scowled, hoisting his strap with a huff. "Folks don't go tracking trivial details like that in campfire stories!"

"Hey, don't run off!" Wei Wuxian chuckled, holding up placating hands. "One more question, friend. Xinglu Ridge is still within Qinghe borders, isn't it? And isn't Qinghe the sovereign domain of the Nie Clan? If bloodthirsty monstrosities are really tearing through their backyard, why haven't they lifted a finger?"

This time, rather than another blank shrug, the vendor’s lip curled into pure scorn. "The Nie Clan? Well, if we were talking about the Nie Clan of the old days, they wouldn't have stood for it for a second. The day after a rumor like that broke, they would've mobilized like lightning and wiped the nest clean off the map. But the fellow running the show now? Heh, isn't he that famous 'Three-Times-Ignorant' Master?"

The former Sect Leader of the Qinghe Nie Clan had been Chifeng-zun, Nie Mingjue. After his father was provoked into an early grave by Wen Ruohan, the tyrant of Qishan, Nie Mingjue had assumed leadership before even coming of age, running the clan with an iron-willed, uncompromising severity. He had formed a sworn brotherhood with Ze-wu-jun Lan Xichen and Lianfang-zun Jin Guangyao. In the aftermath of the Sunshot Campaign, his iron grip had propelled the Nie Clan to dizzying heights, their renown briefly eclipsing even the Lanling Jin Clan.

Yet when his spiritual cultivation suffered catastrophic backlash—erupting into madness before dying in a horrific, bloody public meltdown—the mantle had fallen squarely upon the shoulders of his younger brother, Nie Huaisang.

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. "Why the moniker 'Three-Times-Ignorant'?"

"You haven't heard that one?" the vendor scoffed. "With this Sect Leader Nie, if he doesn't know an answer, he won't speak; if hedoesknow, he’s too scared to breathe a word. Push him too hard or corner him on a tough issue, and he’ll start shaking his head, blubbering through tears:'I don't know, I don't know, I really don't know anything!'practically begging on his knees to be let off the hook. If that isn't 'Three-Times-Ignorant,' what is?"

Having shared desks with Nie Huaisang back in their student days, Wei Wuxian could certainly vouch for the man's character. Nie Huaisang wasn't a bad person, and he was far from stupid. His problem was that he had zero interest in scholarship or cultivation; every ounce of his brilliance went into worldly pleasures—painting fans, netting songbirds, cutting class, and catching fish. When it came to martial arts, his natural aptitude was so disastrously sluggish that he’d lagged eight or nine years behind his peers just to condense a golden core.

During his lifetime, Nie Mingjue had run himself ragged trying to whip the boy into shape, disciplining him with relentless severity, yet the kid remained hopeless. With his elder brother no longer around to run interference and hold up the sky, the Qinghe Nie Clan under Nie Huaisang's reign had made dazzling strides—straight downhill.

Reaching adulthood, and especially after inheriting the sect, Nie Huaisang found himself perpetually swamped by clan business he didn't understand, running across the realm begging for bailouts. He relied entirely on his late brother’s sworn siblings: bawling to Jin Guangyao atop Carp Tower on Monday, then sniffling to Lan Xichen in Cloud Recesses on Tuesday. It was solely because the heads of the Jin and Lan clans perpetually had his back that he managed to keep his seat. These days, whenever people brought up Nie Huaisang, polite etiquette kept them quiet, but their faces practically screamed four words:completely, utterly useless.

Drifting back into the past always left a bittersweet ache in the throat.

His curiosity sated, Wei Wuxian threw the peddler a bone, purchasing two jars of cheap rouge before ambling back to Lan Wangji’s side. The man didn't make a single move to ask for his coin pouch back, silently taking the lead as they set off toward the direction the vendor had indicated.

Xinglu Ridge was blanketed by a sweeping expanse of fir forest. The trails were broad and the canopy rustled with a brisk, clean breeze; yet after trekking through the greenery for quite some time, they failed to turn up a single anomaly. Then again, neither of them had pinned much hope on the excursion; they’d only made the climb just to be thorough. If a terrifying rumor held any water, there were usually concrete specifics to back it up. When the Soul-Consuming Goddess terrorized Dafan Mountain, the victims' names and addresses were common knowledge, right down to the pet names used for A-Yan’s fiancé. When locals were entirely evasive regarding the identities of the devoured, nine times out of ten the tale was pure hot air spun to rattle travelers.

After roughly half an incense stick of walking, their trek finally hit a minor snag.

Shuffling out from the timber ahead were seven or eight ragged silhouettes. Rolling their eyes back, garments shredded, they drifted like twigs about to be toppled by the breeze—a procession of bottom-of-the-barrel walking corpses moving at a crawl.

Creatures this weak sat at the absolute bottom of the undead food chain. A sturdy farmer could kick an entire line of them over with one boot; an energetic toddler could leave them in the dust in half a block. Even in the absolute worst-case scenario where one managed to snag you and take a couple bites of vitality, it wouldn't kill you. Aside from being hideous to look at and smelling rank, they posed zero threat. High-tier cultivators on a night-hunt generally ignored them entirely, leaving them for raw recruits to practice on—the same way a hunter stalks tigers and leopards rather than wasting arrows on mice.

Wei Wuxian knew trouble was coming the second he spotted them and ducked smoothly behind Lan Wangji’s back. Sure enough, the shambling corpses meandered to within thirty paces, caught sight of Wei Wuxian, and froze. Instantly terror-stricken, they wheeled around and sprinted the other way, their legs churning twice as fast as when they’d approached.

Wei Wuxian rubbed his temples, popping out from behind Lan Wangji’s sleeve with feigned awe. "Heavens, Hanguang-jun, you are truly magnificent! The second they caught a glimpse of your majesty, they turned tail and ran for dear life! Ahaha."

Lan Wangji stared at him in deadpan silence.

Wei Wuxian gave his shoulder a breezy shove. "Come on, let's head down the ridge. Clearly there's nothing else lurking around here. The locals sure love to spin yarns—exaggerating a few pathetic stiffs into bone-eating horrors! That 'Man-Eating Castle' is definitely a fairy tale. Total wild goose chase!"

Pushed along, Lan Wangji finally began to walk. Before Wei Wuxian could catch his stride, a furious chorus of barking tore through the distant fir trees.

Wei Wuxian went white as a sheet. In a heartbeat, he bolted behind Lan Wangji, wrapping both arms around the man's waist and shrinking into a tight, trembling ball.

Lan Wangji stood entirely still. "...It is still far off. What are you hiding from?"

"Hide first, ask questions later!" Wei Wuxian hissed, teeth chattering. "Where is it?! Where is it coming from?!"

Lan Wangji listened to the wind for a beat. "It is Jin Ling’s spiritual hound."

Hearing the boy's name, Wei Wuxian tried to stand, only for another violent howl to send his knees buckling right back to the dirt.

Lan Wangji’s voice was calm. "The hound is barking wildly. It must have encountered something."

Wei Wuxian wept inwardly, forcing his quivering legs to hoist him upright. "T-t-then... let's go check it out!"

Lan Wangji didn't move an inch.

Wei Wuxian urged, "Hanguang-jun, move! Take a step! If you stay planted here, what am I supposed to do?!"

A heavy silence lingered before Lan Wangji spoke, his voice dropping slightly: "You... let go first."

Tangled together in an awkward, stumbling shuffle, they traced the sound through the timber, only to find themselves looping through the fir trees twice. The frantic barking sounded close one second, then impossibly distant the next. Having endured the howling for this long, Wei Wuxian’s nerves finally leveled out enough for him to drop the stammer. "Is there a labyrinth array around here?"

The ward was clearly artificial. Considering they’d just dismissed the tales of Xinglu Ridge as cheap gossip, things were suddenly getting interesting.

The hound kept up its booming barks for half an incense stick without losing steam. Cracking the illusionary boundary, the two pushed past the disorienting mist, and before long, the ominous silhouettes of sprawling stone fortresses emerged from the shadows of the fir grove.

The structures were assembled from pale, chalky stone blocks, draped in clinging wild vines and dead leaves. Strangely, each fortress was shaped into a peculiar dome, resembling gigantic stone bowls inverted over the earth.

There really were stone fortresses hidden away in Xinglu Ridge. It seemed the rumors weren't entirely baseless. But whether this place was actually a "Man-Eating Castle"—and what kind of monstrosities resided inside—remained to be seen.

Jin Ling’s black-maned hound was pacing the perimeter of the stone complex, alternating between low growls and frantic barks. Seeing Lan Wangji approach, it shrank back a few steps in instinctive fear, but it didn't flee. Instead, it barked even louder at the pair, glancing back toward the dome while digging violently at the soil with its front paws, kicking dirt into the air in a state of frantic distress.

Cowering behind Lan Wangji’s shoulder, Wei Wuxian groaned, "Why isn't it running away... Where's its master?! Where did Jin Ling go?!"

From the moment the barking began to this very second, they hadn't heard a peep from Jin Ling—not even a cry for help. The dog had undoubtedly guided the boy here and cracked the maze, yet the living person had seemingly evaporated into thin air.

Lan Wangji said, "Let us look inside."

Wei Wuxian blinked. "Look inside how? There are no doors."

He wasn't exaggerating. The chalk-white stonework was sealed completely flush, without a single opening for a door or a window. The hound let out a series of whines and leaped up, looking like it wanted to nip at Lan Wangji’s hem. Hesitating in fear of the man, it swerved and clamped its jaws onto the hem of Wei Wuxian’s robes instead, dragging him backward with all its might!

Wei Wuxian’s soul nearly rocketed out of his throat. He threw both hands out toward the white robes ahead of him. "Lan Zhan... Lan Zhan, Lan Zhan... Lan Zhan, Lan Zhan, Lan Zhan!!!"

The hound dragged Wei Wuxian, Wei Wuxian dragged Lan Wangji, and the dog wound up hauling both grown men around the curved base of the stone dome.

Around the back, an opening nearly as tall as a man gaped in the masonry. The edges were jagged and uneven, surrounded by fresh rubble—clearly blown apart moments ago by a high-grade spiritual blast. The interior was pitch-black, faintly tinged with a murky reddish aura. Releasing its grip, the hound barked violently into the breach, then whipped around to wag its tail frantically at the two cultivators.

No explanation was needed: Jin Ling had blasted his way inside, only to run straight into foul play.

Bichen slid half an inch from its scabbard, the blade radiating an icy azure halo that cut through the darkness. Ducking slightly, Lan Wangji stepped through the breach first. Driven half-mad by the dog hovering behind his heels, Wei Wuxian tumbled inside after him, nearly crashing into his back. Lan Wangji caught his hand to steady him, giving his head a faint, resigned shake.

The hound clearly wanted to follow, scrabbling desperately to cross the threshold, but some unseen barrier repelled it, bouncing the animal back no matter how hard it pushed. Defeated, it sat outside the breach, its tail whipping the dirt in an anxious flurry. Wei Wuxian was so relieved he nearly dropped to his knees in gratitude.

Reclaiming his hand, he took several steps inward. Against the pitch-black shadows of the fortress, the chilling blue glare of the sword transformed into a stark, snowy white.

The mountain forest had been damp and cool, but the interior of the fortress was bone-chilling. Clad in thin robes, the draft bit straight through Wei Wuxian’s sleeves and back, instantly chilling the cold sweat the dog had scared out of him. The ambient light from the opening had long since faded like an extinguished flame; the deeper they stepped, the wider the interior yawned, and the heavier the darkness pressed in.

The domed ceiling arched high overhead. Kicking a loose stone, Wei Wuxian caught the faint, hollow whisper of an echo.

Finally, he couldn't take it anymore. Halting in his tracks, he pressed his right hand against his temple, his brows pinching tight.

Lan Wangji turned. "What is it?"

Wei Wuxian muttered, "...It’s deafening."

Inside the fortress, not a breath stirred. It was as dead and suffocating as a tomb—and indeed, it resembled nothing so much as an enormous crypt.

Yet in Wei Wuxian’s ears, the air was shrieking with an overwhelming, chaotic roar.
